title: The Picture of Dorian Gray
author: Oscar Wilde
summary: Na Londres elegante do fim do século XIX, o pintor Basil Hallward termina o retrato de um jovem de beleza extraordinária, Dorian Gray. Influenciado pelas ideias sedutoras de Lord Henry Wotton, Dorian deseja que o quadro envelheça em seu lugar. O desejo parece se realizar, e o retrato começa a guardar segredos que ninguém deve ver.

chapters.title: The Painter and the Young Man
paragraphs: The studio was full of the smell of roses. Through the open window came the sound of bees and the distant noise of London. In the middle of the room stood a portrait of a young man of extraordinary beauty, and in front of it sat the painter, Basil Hallward, looking at his work with quiet pleasure.

Lord Henry Wotton lay on a sofa, smoking one cigarette after another. He was a clever, lazy man with a soft voice, and he loved to say shocking things simply to see what effect they had. “It is your best work, Basil,” he said. “You must send it to the Grosvenor next year. Everyone will talk about it.”
“I don't think I shall send it anywhere,” Basil answered.
Lord Henry raised his eyebrows. “Not send it anywhere? My dear fellow, why not? There is only one thing in the world worse than being talked about, and that is not being talked about.”
“I know you will laugh at me,” said Basil, “but I really can't exhibit it. I have put too much of myself into it.”

Lord Henry laughed. “Too much of yourself? I don't see any likeness between you and this young Adonis. You are clever and you have a strong, rough face. He is made of ivory and rose leaves. Who is he?”
Basil hesitated before he answered. “His name is Dorian Gray. I didn't intend to tell you. When I like people very much, I never tell their names to anyone. It is like giving away a part of them.”

He got up and walked around the garden with his friend, and at last he explained. Two months earlier, at a crowded party, he had turned round and seen Dorian Gray for the first time. “Our eyes met,” he said, “and I felt that I was growing pale. A strange feeling of terror came over me. I knew that this young man had such a powerful personality that, if I allowed it, it would absorb my whole nature, my whole soul, my very art itself.”
“And what happened then?”

“We were introduced. Since then I have seen him every day. I couldn't be happy if I didn't see him. He is all my art to me now. His face has shown me a new way of painting, a new way of seeing the world. That is why I won't show the portrait. People would look at it and guess my secret.”
“You are very romantic,” said Lord Henry with a smile. “I must meet this young man.”

“I don't want you to meet him,” said Basil seriously. “You have a bad influence on everyone, Harry, although you never do anything wrong yourself. Dorian has a simple and beautiful nature. Don't spoil him. Don't try to influence him.”
At that moment the butler came into the garden. “Mr. Dorian Gray is in the studio, sir,” he said.
Lord Henry laughed. “You must introduce me now, Basil. You have no choice.”

Basil turned to him with a look of real anxiety. “Remember what I have asked you, Harry. Don't take away from me the one person who gives my art whatever charm it possesses. My life as an artist depends on him.”
“What nonsense you talk!” said Lord Henry, and taking his friend by the arm, he led him back into the house.

chapters.title: A Dangerous Wish
paragraphs: Dorian Gray was sitting at the piano, turning the pages of some music. He was indeed wonderfully handsome, with curved red lips, frank blue eyes and golden hair. There was something in his face that made people trust him at once: all the innocence and the passionate purity of youth.
“You must lend me these, Basil,” he cried, and then he saw Lord Henry and blushed.

Basil introduced them, and Lord Henry was charming at once. While Dorian stood on the platform for the painting, Lord Henry talked. He talked about life, about pleasure, about the need to live completely. “The only way to get rid of a temptation is to yield to it,” he said. “Resist it, and your soul grows sick with longing for the things it has forbidden to itself.”

Dorian listened, and his heart began to beat fast. Nobody had ever spoken to him like this. The words seemed to touch some secret part of him that he had never known. Basil painted on in silence, noticing only that a wonderful new expression had come into the boy's face.

After a while they went out into the garden. Dorian buried his face in the lilac blossoms, and Lord Henry watched him. “You have a wonderfully beautiful face, Mr. Gray,” he said. “Don't frown. You have. And beauty is a form of genius. But youth is the one thing worth having, and it lasts such a little time. In a few years your hair will lose its gold, your cheeks will become hollow and your eyes dull. You will suffer horribly. Live while you can! Be afraid of nothing. A new pleasure is what our century wants, and you might be its visible symbol.”
Dorian grew pale. He looked frightened, and Lord Henry was pleased by the effect of his words.
When they went back into the studio, Basil put the last touches to the portrait and stepped back. “It is quite finished,” he said, and he signed his name in thin red letters in the corner.
Lord Henry looked at the picture carefully. “My dear Basil, it is the finest portrait of modern times. Mr. Gray, come and look at yourself.”

Dorian walked slowly to the picture. When he saw it, his cheeks flushed with pleasure. He stood there without moving, as if he were recognising himself for the first time. Then he remembered Lord Henry's words about youth and age, and a sharp pain went through him.

“How sad it is!” he murmured, with his eyes still on the portrait. “I shall grow old, and horrible, and dreadful. But this picture will remain always young. It will never be older than this particular day of June. If only it were the other way! If it were I who was to be always young, and the picture that was to grow old! For that, I would give everything. Yes, there is nothing in the whole world I would not give. I would give my soul for that!”
“You would hardly care for such an arrangement, Basil,” said Lord Henry, laughing.

But Dorian turned to the painter in anger. “I am jealous of everything whose beauty does not die. I am jealous of the portrait you have painted of me. Why should it keep what I must lose? Every moment that passes takes something from me and gives something to it.” Tears came into his eyes, and he threw himself on the sofa.
“This is your doing, Harry,” said Basil bitterly. He picked up a long palette knife and walked towards the canvas. “I will not let it come across our three lives and ruin them. I shall destroy it.”
Dorian jumped up with a cry and seized the knife from his hand. “Don't, Basil, don't! It would be murder!”
“I am glad you appreciate my work at last,” said Basil coldly, when he had recovered from his surprise. “It shall be varnished and framed and sent home to you.”
That evening Dorian went to the theatre with Lord Henry, although Basil had begged him to stay. Basil was left alone with the picture, and he felt that he had lost something.

chapters.title: Sibyl Vane
paragraphs: A month later, Lord Henry was waiting in Dorian's library when the young man came in, late and excited. “Harry, I am in love,” he said at once. “I am in love with an actress.”
“People who love only once in their lives are really shallow,” said Lord Henry lightly. “Tell me about her.”

Dorian sat down, his face bright with emotion. He explained that one evening he had wandered through the dirty streets of East London, looking for adventure. He had come to a cheap little theatre, and a horrible old man with a great diamond in his shirt had offered him a box. “I almost left,” Dorian said. “The scenery was ugly, and the audience was eating oranges and cracking nuts. They were playing Romeo and Juliet. Romeo was a fat old man, and I was bored. But then Juliet came on the stage.”

His voice trembled. “Harry, imagine a girl, hardly seventeen, with a little flower-like face, a small Greek head with dark brown hair, eyes like violet wells of passion, lips like the petals of a rose. She was the loveliest thing I had ever seen in my life. And her voice! I have never heard such a voice. Her name is Sibyl Vane.”
“And you have been there every night since?”

“Every night. One night she is Rosalind, the next evening she is Imogen. I have seen her die in the gloom of an Italian tomb. She is never the same. Ordinary women never appeal to one's imagination, but an actress is different. She is all the great heroines of the world in one.”
“When did you first speak to her?”

“On the third night. The old Jew, the manager, took me behind the scenes. She was so shy. She looked at me as if I were something wonderful, and she called me Prince Charming. She doesn't know my real name. She lives with her mother, a tired, faded woman, and she has a brother who is going to sea.”

Lord Henry smiled. He was fascinated, not by the girl, but by the boy. He saw that his own words had awakened something in Dorian, and he wished to observe what would happen, as a scientist observes an experiment. “And what are you going to do?” he asked.

“I want you and Basil to come with me some night and see her act. I have not the slightest fear of the result. You will recognise her genius. Then we must get her away from that terrible manager. She is bound to him for three years, but I shall pay him. I shall take a West End theatre and bring her out properly. She will make the world as mad as she has made me.”
“That would be impossible, my dear boy.”
“Yes, she will. She has not only art, consummate art, but she has personality also. And you have often told me that it is personalities, not principles, that move the age.”

After Dorian had gone, Lord Henry sat thinking. It was clear to him that the young man's soul was coming to life, and that he himself had helped to create it. When he arrived home late that night, he found a telegram on the hall table. He opened it and read that Dorian Gray was engaged to be married to Sibyl Vane.

chapters.title: The Sailor's Warning
paragraphs: In a shabby room in a poor part of London, Sibyl Vane was holding her mother's hands. “Mother, I am so happy,” she said. “You must be happy too.”

Mrs. Vane looked at her daughter with anxious eyes. She had been an actress herself and she had lived through many years of hardship. “Happy? I am only happy when I see you act. You must think of nothing but your acting. Mr. Isaacs has been very good to us, and we owe him money.”
“Money, Mother? What does money matter? Love is more than money.” Sibyl's face shone. She was thinking of Prince Charming, and she was afraid of nothing.

Just then the door opened and a young man with rough brown hair came in. This was her brother James. He was thick-set and badly dressed, and he looked unhappy. He was leaving for Australia the next day as a sailor. He asked Sibyl to come for a walk with him in the park, since it would be their last chance.
As they walked, Sibyl talked only of her lover. “He is so wonderful, Jim. He is a gentleman, and I love him.”
James frowned. “You don't even know his name. I want you to beware of him. Gentlemen like that only want to amuse themselves with girls like you.”
At that moment an open carriage passed them, and Sibyl cried out, “There he is! Look, Jim! Prince Charming!” But by the time James turned his head, the carriage had gone, and he did not see the face.
“I wish I had seen him,” said James darkly. “Because, as sure as there is a God in heaven, if he ever does you any wrong, I shall kill him.”
Sibyl looked at him in horror. “You are mad, Jim. You are jealous and unkind. Oh, I wish you were in love too!”
That evening, before he left, James asked his mother a question that he had been wanting to ask for weeks. “Mother, were you married to my father?”

Mrs. Vane looked at the floor. “No,” she whispered. “He was a gentleman, and he was not free. He died before he could help us.” James swore under his breath. He made his mother promise that she would watch over Sibyl, and then he went out into the night with his small bag on his shoulder.
The next day, Lord Henry met Basil Hallward at his club and gave him the news. “Dorian Gray is engaged to be married.”
Basil started and frowned. “To whom?”
“To a little actress, Sibyl Vane.”
“I can't believe it. Dorian is far too sensible.”
“Dorian is far too wise not to do foolish things now and then, my dear Basil.”

That evening the three of them had dinner together, and Dorian was radiant. He told them how he had kissed Sibyl after her performance as Rosalind. “Harry, I forgot all your wrong, fascinating theories when I was with her. When I am with her, I regret all that you have taught me. I become different from what you have known me to be.” Then they drove together to the little theatre to see her act. Basil sat in the carriage alone and felt a strange sadness, as if Dorian could never again be to him all that he had been in the past.

chapters.title: A Terrible Performance
paragraphs: The theatre was crowded that night, and the heat was terrible. Young men in their shirt sleeves shouted to each other across the hall, and women laughed loudly in the cheap seats. Lord Henry looked around with amusement. “What a place to find one's divinity in!” he said.

“Yes,” said Dorian proudly. “It was here I found her, and she is divine beyond all living things. When she acts, you will forget everything. These common people become quiet and listen to her. She makes them cry and laugh as she wishes.”

At last the curtain rose, and Sibyl Vane came on the stage. Lord Henry had to admit that she was lovely to look at. But as soon as she began to speak, something was wrong. Her voice was beautiful, but it was completely false. She spoke the wonderful lines of Juliet like a schoolgirl who has learnt a lesson. The passion had gone out of her. She was stiff and artificial.

Dorian grew pale. He sat watching her, and his hands shook. In the balcony scene, which should have been the most beautiful part, she was simply bad. The audience began to talk loudly and to whistle. Even the manager, standing at the back, swore in anger.
At the end of the second act, Lord Henry stood up and put on his coat. “She is quite beautiful, Dorian,” he said, “but she can't act. Let us go.”
“I am going to stay to the end,” said Dorian in a hard, bitter voice. “I am awfully sorry that I have made you waste an evening, Harry.”
Basil spoke gently. “My dear Dorian, she must be ill. We will come some other night.”

“I wish she were ill,” Dorian answered. “But she seems to me to be simply callous and cold. She has entirely altered. Last night she was a great artist. This evening she is merely a commonplace actress.”

When his friends had gone, Dorian sat through the rest of the play in agony. As soon as it was over, he rushed behind the scenes. Sibyl was standing there alone, with a look of triumph on her face. Her eyes were shining.
“How badly I acted tonight, Dorian!” she cried happily.
“Horribly!” he answered, staring at her in amazement. “It was dreadful. Are you ill? You have no idea what I suffered.”

The girl smiled. “Dorian, don't you understand? Before I knew you, acting was the one reality of my life. I lived only in the theatre. I thought it was all true. Then you came, and you freed my soul from prison. You taught me what reality really is. Tonight, for the first time, I saw the emptiness of the play. The painted scenery was ugly, and Romeo was old. The words were not real. I could not pretend any more. I have seen something higher. What do I care for the shadows of love, when I have love itself? You are more to me than all art can ever be.”
He threw himself down on the sofa and turned away his face. “You have killed my love,” he said quietly.
She looked at him in wonder, and laughed. He did not answer. She came to him and touched his hair with her little fingers. He pushed her away.

“Yes,” he cried, “you have killed my love. You used to stir my imagination. Now you don't even stir my curiosity. I loved you because you were marvellous, because you had genius and intellect, because you gave shape and substance to the shadows of art. You have thrown it all away. You are shallow and stupid. I will never see you again. I will never think of you. What are you now? A third-rate actress with a pretty face.”
Sibyl fell at his feet and lay there like a broken flower. “Dorian, don't leave me!” she whispered. “I will work so hard. I will try to improve. Don't go away from me. I couldn't bear it.”

But he looked down at her with contempt. “I am going,” he said at last in his calm, clear voice. “I don't wish to be unkind, but I can't see you again. You have disappointed me.” And he left the theatre and walked through the dark streets until dawn.

chapters.title: The Changed Face
paragraphs: It was already light when Dorian arrived home. As he passed through the library towards his bedroom, his eyes fell on the portrait that Basil had painted of him. He stopped in surprise. The face seemed to him to be a little changed. The expression looked different. One would have said that there was a touch of cruelty in the mouth.

He turned on the light and looked again. It was certainly true. In the clear morning light, the lines of cruelty round the mouth were plain to see. It was as if he had looked into a mirror after he had done some dreadful thing.

He threw himself into a chair and began to think. Suddenly he remembered what he had said in Basil's studio on the day the picture had been finished. He had wished that he himself might remain young, and that the portrait might grow old. Surely such a wish could not have come true? Such things were impossible. And yet, there was the picture, with that touch of cruelty in the mouth.

Cruelty! Had he been cruel? He thought of Sibyl Vane lying at his feet, sobbing like a little child. He had been cruel. But she had hurt him too. Then he looked at the picture again, and a feeling of terrible pity came over him, not for her, but for himself. The portrait would be to him the visible emblem of his conscience. It would show him his own soul.

“I will not sin again,” he said to himself. “I will go back to Sibyl. I will make her amends, marry her, and try to love her again.” He drew a screen in front of the picture, so that he would not have to see it, and went to bed.

It was long past noon when he woke. He felt calmer. He wrote a long, passionate letter to Sibyl, asking her to forgive him. When he had finished, he felt that he had been forgiven already. Just then there was a knock at the door, and Lord Henry came in.
“My dear boy,” he said, “I am so sorry for you. But you must not think too much about it. Have you seen her?”
“Do you mean Sibyl Vane? Yes, I was brutal to her, Harry. But it is all right now. I am going to marry her. I have written to her.”
Lord Henry looked at him strangely. “Marry Sibyl Vane? But, Dorian, haven't you read the newspapers? Didn't you get my letter? Sibyl Vane is dead.”
A cry of pain broke from Dorian's lips. “Dead! Sibyl dead! It is not true! It is a horrible lie!”

“It is quite true. It is in all the morning papers. She was found dead on the floor of her dressing room. She seems to have swallowed something by mistake, some dreadful poison they use at theatres. I suppose it was suicide. There will be an inquest, of course, but you must not be mixed up in it. Nobody at the theatre knows your name, I hope?”

Dorian was silent for a long time. “So I have murdered Sibyl Vane,” he said at last, half to himself. “Murdered her as surely as if I had cut her little throat with a knife. And yet the roses are not less lovely. The birds sing just as happily in my garden. And tonight I am to dine with you, and then go to the opera. How extraordinarily dramatic life is!”

Lord Henry smiled. “You must think of it as a wonderful scene in a tragedy,” he said softly. “The girl never really lived, and so she has never really died. To you at least she was always a dream. Don't waste your tears on Sibyl Vane. Mourn for Ophelia, if you like. Mourn for Juliet. But she was less real than they are.”

Dorian looked up and felt comforted. “I think you are right, Harry. You have explained me to myself.” When Lord Henry had gone, Dorian pulled the screen aside and looked at the portrait once more. There was no further change. He realised that the picture would bear the weight of everything he did. Eternal youth, endless passion, wild joys and wilder sins: he was to have all these things. The portrait was to bear the burden of his shame. That was all.

chapters.title: The Locked Room
paragraphs: The next morning, Basil Hallward came to see Dorian. He was pale and upset. “I have been looking for you since last night,” he said. “I read the terrible news. I went to the theatre and to your house, but you were at the opera. How could you go to the opera, Dorian, when Sibyl Vane was lying dead?”
“Stop, Basil! I won't hear it!” cried Dorian, jumping up. “What is past is past. You must not tell me about things. What is done is done.”

Basil stared at him. “You call yesterday the past? Dorian, this is horrible! Something has changed you completely. You look exactly the same wonderful boy, but you talk as if you had no heart, no pity in you. It is all Harry's influence. I see that.”

Dorian turned away and looked out at the garden. “I owe a great deal to Harry,” he said at last. “More than I owe to you. You only taught me to be vain.” Then he became gentle again. “Basil, don't talk to me about horrible subjects. Don't leave me now. I am changed, but you must always be my friend.”

The painter was moved, and he gave up arguing. After a while he said, “Well, Dorian, I want you to sit for me again. And you must let me look at my portrait. Why have you put that screen in front of it?” He began to walk across the room.

A cry of terror broke from Dorian's lips, and he rushed between Basil and the screen. “Basil, you must not look at it. I don't wish you to. If you try to look at it, I will never speak to you again as long as I live. I am quite serious.”
Basil was astonished. “But why? I want to exhibit it in Paris in the autumn. That is one of the reasons I came.”
“Exhibit it! Never!” Dorian was pale with fear. Then a thought came to him. “Basil, you once told me there was a reason why you would never exhibit it. Tell me that reason.”

So Basil told him. He confessed that from the moment they had met, Dorian had dominated his life and his art. “I worshipped you,” he said simply. “I was afraid that the world would see my idolatry in the picture. Now that I have told you, I feel that I was foolish. You must never let me look at it again, if you wish it.” And he went away, feeling that something had died between them.

As soon as he had gone, Dorian knew that he had to hide the portrait at once. Nobody must ever see it. He took the key of the old schoolroom at the top of the house, a room that nobody had used for years. He ordered two men to carry the heavy picture up the stairs, covered with a purple cloth. When they had gone, he locked the door and put the key in his pocket. Now he felt safe. No eye but his would ever see his shame.

When he came down to the library, he found a yellow book lying on the table, a present from Lord Henry. He opened it and began to read. It was a strange novel without a plot, the story of a young Parisian who spent his life trying to experience every passion and every sin of the past centuries. The style was rich and poisonous. Dorian read it for hours, until it was too dark to see.

For years afterwards, Dorian could not free himself from the influence of this book. He bought nine copies of the first edition and had them bound in different colours, to suit his changing moods. The hero of the novel seemed to him to be a kind of picture of himself. The whole book seemed to contain the story of his own life, written before he had lived it.

chapters.title: Eighteen Years
paragraphs: The years passed, and Dorian Gray did not change. At twenty, at thirty, at thirty-eight, he still had the face of a boy of twenty, pure and bright and innocent. People who heard the strangest stories about him could not believe them when they saw him. He had the look of one who had kept himself unspotted from the world.

But the stories were many. He was seen in the worst parts of London, in dirty taverns and opium dens. Young men who had been his friends had been ruined. One had killed himself; another had been forced to leave England. Women's names had been lost because of him. Some gentlemen left the room when he came into their club. And yet he was rich, charming and beautiful, and society forgave him much.

Dorian lived for pleasure. He studied perfumes and music, jewels and embroideries. He gave magnificent dinners. But often, after a long absence, he would creep upstairs to the locked room and stand in front of the portrait. He would look first at the evil, ageing face on the canvas and then at the fair young face that laughed back at him from the mirror. The face in the picture was growing old and cruel. Its mouth was heavy, its eyes were evil. And sometimes Dorian felt not horror but a monstrous pride in his secret.

It was on the ninth of November, the eve of his thirty-eighth birthday, that he walked home at eleven o'clock through a cold, thick fog. In the street a man passed him, carrying a bag, and Dorian recognised him. It was Basil Hallward. A strange sense of fear came over him, but Basil had already seen him.

“Dorian! What an extraordinary piece of luck!” said Basil. “I have been waiting for you in your library. I am going to Paris by the midnight train, and I wanted to see you before I left. I have something important to say to you.”
They went into the house together. Basil put down his bag and spoke seriously. “Dorian, I want to speak to you about the things that people are saying about you in London. Terrible things.”
“I don't wish to hear them,” said Dorian lazily. “I love scandals about other people, but scandals about myself don't interest me.”

“They must interest you, Dorian. Every gentleman is interested in his good name. Of course, I don't believe these rumours. Sin is a thing that writes itself across a man's face. It cannot be hidden. And your face is pure. But why is your friendship so fatal to young men? Why did Lord Staveley's son have to leave England? What about Adrian Singleton and his dreadful end? What about the young Duke of Perth? People say you go to dreadful places at night. I wonder whether I know you at all. To answer that, I should have to see your soul.”
“To see my soul!” muttered Dorian, starting up from the sofa and turning almost white with fear.
“Yes,” answered Basil seriously, with deep sorrow in his voice. “To see your soul. But only God can do that.”

A bitter laugh came from the lips of the younger man. “You shall see it yourself, tonight!” he cried. “Come. It is your own work. Why shouldn't you look at it? You can tell the world all about it afterwards, if you choose. Nobody would believe you.”
“You must not say things like that, Dorian. It is blasphemy.”
“Come upstairs, Basil,” Dorian said quietly. “I keep a diary of my life from day to day, and it never leaves the room in which it is written. I shall show it to you if you come with me.”
“I shall come with you, Dorian, if you wish it,” said Basil. “I see I have missed my train. That makes no difference. I can go tomorrow.”

chapters.title: Murder and the Chemist
paragraphs: They climbed the stairs in silence. The lamp threw strange shadows on the walls. At the top, Dorian unlocked the door of the old schoolroom. A cold current of air passed them. The room looked as if it had not been lived in for years. Dust lay over everything, and a mouse ran away behind the old furniture.
“So you think that only God sees the soul, Basil?” said Dorian in a hard voice. “Draw that curtain back, and you will see mine.”

Basil frowned and pulled the purple cloth from the picture. An exclamation of horror broke from his lips. In the dim light he saw a hideous face grinning at him from the canvas. There was something in its expression that filled him with disgust and loathing. Good heavens! It was Dorian Gray's own face that he was looking at. The horror had not yet entirely spoilt that marvellous beauty. There was still some gold in the thinning hair and some red on the sensual mouth. Yes, it was Dorian himself. But who had done it? He recognised his own brushwork, and in the corner was his own name in long red letters.
“What does this mean?” he cried at last, in a strange, cold voice.

“Years ago, when I was a boy,” said Dorian, “you met me, flattered me, and taught me to be vain of my good looks. One day you finished a portrait of me that revealed to me the wonder of beauty. In a mad moment, that I don't know even now whether I regret or not, I made a wish. Perhaps you would call it a prayer.”
“I remember it! Oh, how well I remember it! No, the thing is impossible. The room is damp. The paints I used had some poison in them. I tell you, the thing is impossible.”
“Ah, what is impossible?” murmured the young man.

Basil looked again at the picture. “My God! If it is true, and this is what you have done with your life, then you must be worse even than those who talk against you imagine you to be.” He sank into a chair and put his face in his hands. “Pray, Dorian, pray,” he whispered. “What is it that one was taught to say in one's boyhood? ‘Lead us not into temptation. Forgive us our sins.’ Let us say that together. The prayer of your pride has been answered. The prayer of your repentance will be answered also.”
“It is too late, Basil,” said Dorian.

He glanced at the picture, and suddenly an uncontrollable feeling of hatred for Basil Hallward came over him, as though it had been suggested to him by the image on the canvas. The mad passions of a hunted animal stirred within him, and he hated the man at the table more than he had ever hated anything in his life. His eye fell on a knife that lay on top of a painted chest. He had brought it up some days before to cut a piece of cord.

He moved slowly towards it, passing Basil as he did so. As soon as he was behind him, he seized the knife and turned round. Basil moved in his chair as if he were going to rise. Dorian rushed at him and dug the knife into the great vein that is behind the ear, crushing the man's head down on the table and stabbing again and again.
There was a terrible choking sound, and the cry of someone drowning in blood. Twice the arms shot up, waving grotesquely. Then the body was still. Something began to drip slowly onto the floor.

Dorian threw the knife on the table and listened. He could hear nothing but the drip, drip on the old carpet. He opened the door and went out onto the landing. The house was absolutely quiet. Nobody was about.

How quickly it had all been done! He felt strangely calm. He locked the door behind him and crept quietly downstairs. He took Basil's bag and coat and hid them in a secret cupboard. Basil had said that he was going to Paris by the midnight train. Everyone would think that he had gone. Months would pass before anyone suspected anything. Then he went out of the house, rang the bell as if he had just come home, and his servant opened the door, half asleep. “Has anyone called this evening?” Dorian asked casually. “Mr. Hallward, sir. He stayed until eleven, and then he went away to catch his train.”

The next morning, Dorian woke late and lay in bed for a long time, smiling, as if he had been lost in some delightful dream. Then, slowly, the memory came back to him. He saw again the room upstairs, the dead man at the table, and he felt sick. He knew that he must not think about it. He must act.
After breakfast, he wrote two letters. He put one in his pocket and gave the other to his servant. “Take this to 152 Hertford Street,” he said. “If Mr. Campbell is out of town, get his address.”

Alan Campbell was a brilliant young chemist. Five years earlier he and Dorian had been close friends, almost inseparable. Then their friendship had suddenly ended, and now, when they met in society, Campbell always left the room. He had become strangely quiet and seemed to dislike music and pleasure. Nobody knew why.

Dorian waited for an hour, in agony, trying to read poetry. At last the door opened and Campbell came in, very stern and pale. “I promised myself I would never enter your house again,” he said. “But you said it was a matter of life and death.”

“It is a matter of life and death, Alan, and to more than one person,” said Dorian. “Sit down. In a locked room at the top of this house, a room to which nobody but myself has access, a dead man is seated at a table. He has been dead for ten hours now. Don't stir, and don't look at me like that. Who the man is, why he died, how he died, are matters that do not concern you. What you have to do is this: you must destroy the body. Destroy it, and everything that belongs to it, so that not a trace is left. You know chemistry. You can do it.”
“You are mad, Dorian. I won't touch it. I don't care what shame comes on you. It is not my business.”
“It was suicide, Alan.”
“I am glad of that. But who drove him to it? You, I should fancy.”
Dorian looked at him for a moment. “Alan, it was murder. I killed him. You don't know what he had made me suffer.”
“Murder! Good God, Dorian, is that what you have come to? I shall not inform upon you. It is not my business. But I will not help you.”

Dorian sighed. Then he took a piece of paper, wrote something on it, folded it and pushed it across the table. Campbell opened it and read it. As he read, his face became ghastly pale, and he fell back in his chair. A horrible sickness came over him. He felt as if his heart was beating itself to death in some empty hollow.

“I am so sorry for you, Alan,” said Dorian gently. “But you leave me no alternative. I have a letter already written. Here it is. You see the address. If you don't help me, I must send it. You know what the result will be. You cannot refuse now.”

Campbell put his face in his hands, and a shudder passed through him. Nobody ever learned what Dorian had written, or what secret it was about Campbell's past. But at last the chemist said, in a broken voice, “I must go home and get some things from my laboratory.”
“No, Alan, you must not leave the house. Write what you need, and my servant will bring them.”

All through the afternoon Campbell worked in the locked room upstairs. Dorian did not go in. Once, when he opened the door to give him the things, he saw that the hand of the figure in the picture was wet with something red, as if the canvas had sweated blood. He shut the door quickly.
It was after seven when Campbell came down, calm but very pale. “I have done what you asked me to do,” he muttered. “And now, goodbye. Let us never see each other again.”
When Dorian went upstairs, there was a horrible smell of chemicals in the room. But the thing that had been sitting at the table was gone.

chapters.title: The Sailor Returns
paragraphs: That night, Dorian went to a dinner party and was more charming than ever. But afterwards he felt a terrible need to forget. He took a carriage and drove to the docks in the east of London, to a place where opium could be bought. There, in the smoke and darkness, he hoped to lose all memory of what he had done.

As he walked into the low room of the opium den, he saw a young man lying on a dirty mattress. It was Adrian Singleton, one of the young friends whose lives he had ruined. Adrian looked up at him and smiled weakly. Dorian could not bear it. He decided to leave and find another place.
As he went out of the door, a woman who was sitting at the bar laughed loudly. “There goes the devil's bargain!” she called after him.
“Curse you!” he answered. “Don't call me that.”
“Prince Charming is what you like to be called, isn't it?” she shouted.

A sailor who had been sleeping at a table woke up suddenly at these words. He looked wildly around and rushed out after Dorian. Dorian was hurrying along the dark, wet street by the river, when suddenly he felt himself seized from behind. Before he could defend himself, he was thrown against the wall, with a strong hand round his throat and a pistol pointing at his head.
“What do you want?” he gasped.

“Keep quiet,” said the man. “If you stir, I shoot you. You wrecked the life of Sibyl Vane. Sibyl Vane was my sister. She killed herself, and I know that her death is at your door. I swore I would kill you in return. For years I have looked for you. I had no clue, no description. I knew only the pet name she used to call you. I heard it tonight by chance. Make your peace with God, for tonight you are going to die.”
Dorian grew sick with fear. Then a wild hope came into his mind. “Stop!” he cried. “How long ago is it since your sister died? Quick, tell me!”
“Eighteen years,” said the man. “Why do you ask me? What do years matter?”
“Eighteen years!” laughed Dorian, with a touch of triumph in his voice. “Eighteen years! Take me under the lamp and look at my face!”

James Vane hesitated for a moment, not understanding what was meant. Then he seized Dorian and dragged him under the street lamp. The light showed the face of a young man of twenty, hardly older than his sister had been when he had left England. It was obvious that this was not the man who had destroyed her life.
He let go and stepped back. “My God! My God!” he cried. “And I would have murdered you!”

Dorian drew a long breath. “You have been on the brink of committing a terrible crime, my man,” he said, looking at him sternly. “Let this be a warning to you not to take vengeance into your own hands.” He turned and walked quickly away.

James Vane stood on the pavement in horror, trembling from head to foot. After a little while, a black shadow came out of the darkness and touched him on the arm. It was the woman from the bar. “Why didn't you kill him?” she whispered. “He has lots of money, and he's as bad as bad.”
“He is not the man I am looking for,” he answered. “The man I want must be nearly forty now. This one is little more than a boy.”
The woman gave a bitter laugh. “Little more than a boy! Why, it's nearly eighteen years since Prince Charming made me what I am.”
“You lie!” cried James Vane.

She raised her hand up to heaven. “Before God I am telling the truth. They say he has sold himself to the devil for a pretty face. It's nearly eighteen years since I met him. He hasn't changed much since then. I have, though.” But when James ran to the corner of the street, Dorian Gray had disappeared.

chapters.title: The Hunter in the Wood
paragraphs: A week later, Dorian was at his country house, Selby Royal, with a party of guests. Lord Henry was there, and a beautiful duchess with whom Dorian liked to talk. One evening, in the conservatory, Dorian suddenly gave a cry and fainted. When he came to himself, he would not say what had happened. But he had seen, pressed against the window, a white face watching him. It was the face of James Vane.

For the next three days he did not leave the house. He spent most of the time in his room, sick with a wild terror of dying. Every shadow seemed to hide a hunter. “I must have imagined it,” he told himself. “Sibyl's brother has gone back to sea. He doesn't know my name. It was only my conscience that made the face.”

On the fourth day he felt braver, and he went out to join a shooting party in the woods. The air was cold and fresh, and the leaves were brown and gold. He walked along beside the Duchess's brother, Sir Geoffrey Clouston, who was carrying a gun.

Suddenly a hare jumped out of the long grass and ran towards the trees. Sir Geoffrey raised his gun. Something in the animal's grace charmed Dorian, and he cried out at once, “Don't shoot it, Geoffrey. Let it live.”

“What nonsense, Dorian!” laughed his companion, and as the hare ran into the bushes, he fired. There were two cries: the cry of a hare in pain, which is dreadful, and the cry of a man in agony, which is worse.
“Good heavens! I have hit a beater!” exclaimed Sir Geoffrey. “What an ass the man was to get in front of the guns!”

The servants dragged a body out into the sunlight. Dorian turned away in horror. It seemed to him that misfortune followed wherever he went. The shooting was stopped for the day, and they walked back to the house. “It is a bad omen,” Dorian said to Lord Henry.
Lord Henry laughed. “Nonsense, my dear Dorian. Nothing is an omen. Destiny does not send us heralds. Besides, what on earth could happen to you? You have everything in the world that a man can want.”
“There is no one with whom I would not change places, Harry,” said Dorian with a sigh. “Don't laugh at me like that. I am telling you the truth.”
That evening, Dorian could not rest. He went down to the cottage where the body of the dead man had been put. “Who was he?” he asked the head keeper. “Was he one of your men?”
“No, sir. Nobody knows who he is. Looks like a sailor, sir. Tattooed on both arms, and that kind of thing.”

Dorian's heart almost stopped. He threw open the door of the cottage and went in. On a heap of sacking in the corner lay the dead body of a man dressed in a coarse shirt. Somebody had placed a handkerchief over his face. Dorian took it away with a trembling hand.
It was the face of James Vane.

He stood there for some minutes looking at the dead body. As he rode home, his eyes were full of tears, for he knew he was safe. The one man who knew his secret, and who had sworn to kill him, was dead, killed by accident in the woods.

chapters.title: The Last Picture
paragraphs: Back in London, Dorian decided to become good. He told Lord Henry that he had done one good action already in the country. He had met a simple village girl called Hetty, who loved him, and he had left her as innocent as he had found her. “I have spared somebody, Harry,” he said. “It is the first good thing I have done for many years.”

Lord Henry smiled. “My dear Dorian, you have broken her heart. She will never again be content with her village life. But tell me, have you heard the latest news? Everyone in London is talking about poor Basil's disappearance. And Alan Campbell has shot himself in his laboratory.”
Dorian grew pale. “What do you think has happened to Basil?” he asked slowly.

“I have not the slightest idea. Perhaps he fell into the Seine, or ran away. I don't think he was murdered. Basil was not clever enough to have enemies. Murder is always a mistake. One should never do anything that one cannot talk about after dinner.” Then he looked at Dorian with interest. “By the way, Dorian, what has become of that wonderful portrait Basil did of you? I wish I could have it.”
“I never really liked it,” said Dorian quickly. “It was stolen, I think, years ago.”

When Lord Henry had gone, Dorian walked home slowly through the warm night. At home he looked at himself in a mirror that Lord Henry had given him long ago. He hated his own beauty. It was his beauty that had ruined him, his beauty and the youth that he had prayed for. He thought of Hetty. Perhaps his good action had already changed the picture. Perhaps the evil look had gone from the face.

He took the lamp and went upstairs. As he unlocked the door, a smile of joy passed across his young face. Yes, he would be good, and the hideous thing that he had hidden away would no longer be a terror to him.

He went in quietly, locked the door behind him, and pulled the purple cloth from the portrait. A cry of pain and anger broke from him. He could see no change, except that in the eyes there was a look of cunning, and in the mouth the curved wrinkle of the hypocrite. The thing was still loathsome, more loathsome, if possible, than before. And the red stain on the hand seemed brighter, more like blood newly spilt.

Had it been merely vanity that had made him do his one good deed? Or the desire for a new sensation, as Lord Henry had hinted? He understood now that he had been lying to himself. He was not sorry. His pretended goodness had been only another mask.

Then he thought of confessing. But who would believe him? There was no trace of the murdered man anywhere. Everything belonging to him had been destroyed. He himself had burned what had been below the stairs. The only evidence left against him was the picture itself.

He looked round and saw the knife that had stabbed Basil Hallward. He had cleaned it many times, until there was no stain left upon it. It was bright, and it shone. As it had killed the painter, so it would kill the painter's work, and all that that meant. It would kill the past, and when that was dead, he would be free. He seized the thing and stabbed the picture with it.

There was a cry heard, and a crash. The cry was so horrible in its agony that the frightened servants woke and crept out of their rooms. Two gentlemen who were passing in the square below stopped and looked up at the great house. They called a policeman, who knocked several times at the door, but there was no answer.

After some time, the servants broke open the door of the locked room. When they entered, they found hanging upon the wall a splendid portrait of their master as they had last seen him, in all the wonder of his exquisite youth and beauty. Lying on the floor was a dead man, in evening dress, with a knife in his heart. He was withered, wrinkled and loathsome of face. It was not till they had examined the rings on his fingers that they recognised who it was.
